title: The Diagonal of Vandermonde: Self-Convolution of a Binomial Row
description: Formalizes the diagonal specialization of Vandermonde's convolution. The general case (m=n, shift d) gives the shifted self-convolution ∑_{k=0}^{n-d} C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) = C(2n,n+d); the d=0 case is the classical sum-of-squares identity ∑_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k)² = C(2n,n) — the sum of the squares of a row of Pascal's triangle equals the central binomial coefficient. Derived from Mathlib's Nat.add_choose_eq by folding the inner coefficient back with the symmetry C(n,(n-d)-k) = C(n,k+d).

meta.author: Lean Genius researcher-5
meta.assumptions: None. The shifted diagonal is stated under the side condition d ≤ n (so n-d and n+d behave classically); the sum-of-squares corollary holds for every natural number n. Both are fully machine-checked and depend only on the foundational axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound (verified via #print axioms — no Lean.ofReduceBool, since the numerical checks use decide rather than native_decide).
originalContributions: sum_choose_mul_choose_shift: the shifted diagonal of Vandermonde, ∑_{k=0}^{n-d} C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) = C(2n,n+d) for d ≤ n, obtained by specializing C(m+n,r) at m=n, r=n-d and folding C(n,(n-d)-k) back to C(n,k+d) via Nat.choose_symm_of_eq_add

sum_sq_choose: the classical sum-of-squares identity ∑_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k)² = C(2n,n) as the d=0 diagonal — the sum of squares of a Pascal row equals the central binomial coefficient — absent elsewhere in the gallery, which records only the bound C(2n,n) ≤ 4^n and row log-concavity
Worked verifications: ∑_{k=0}^{3} C(3,k)² = 20 = C(6,3), ∑_{k=0}^{4} C(4,k)² = 70 = C(8,4), and the shifted case ∑_{k=0}^{2} C(4,k)·C(4,k+2) = 28 = C(8,6), all by axiom-free decide

overview.historicalContext: Vandermonde's convolution C(m+n,r) = ∑_{k=0}^{r} C(m,k)·C(n,r-k) (Chu 1303, Vandermonde 1772) has as its most famous corollary the diagonal case m=n, r=n: ∑_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k)² = C(2n,n). The squares appear because the second factor C(n,n-k) equals C(n,k) by the symmetry of Pascal's triangle. This identity is the n-th term in the generating-function expansion of (1-x)^{-1} via central binomials and underlies the count of lattice paths and the asymptotics C(2n,n) ~ 4^n/√(πn). The shifted version ∑_{k} C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) = C(2n,n+d) is the off-diagonal generalization, equivalently the coefficient extraction [x^{n+d}] (1+x)^n(1+x)^n.
overview.problemStatement: Open Question OQ-10: the general Vandermonde convolution and its Chu–Vandermonde polynomial generalizations are already in the gallery (OQ-01, OQ-01-OQ-02). Formalize the celebrated diagonal specialization — the self-convolution of a single binomial row — in ℕ: the shifted form ∑_{k=0}^{n-d} C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) = C(2n,n+d) for d ≤ n, and its headline d=0 case ∑_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k)² = C(2n,n).
overview.proofStrategy: Specialize Mathlib's Vandermonde Nat.add_choose_eq at both rows equal to n, evaluated at r = n-d, converting the antidiagonal sum to a range sum with Finset.Nat.sum_antidiagonal_eq_sum_range_succ. This yields C(2n,n-d) = ∑_{k=0}^{n-d} C(n,k)·C(n,(n-d)-k). Rewrite each inner coefficient C(n,(n-d)-k) to C(n,k+d) using Nat.choose_symm_of_eq_add applied to the identity n = ((n-d)-k) + (k+d), which omega discharges from k ≤ n-d and d ≤ n. Finally rewrite the closed form C(2n,n-d) = C(2n,n+d) by the same symmetry lemma at 2n = (n-d)+(n+d). The sum-of-squares corollary is the d=0 instance, with k+0 = k and C(n,k)·C(n,k) = C(n,k)² obtained by simp [sq].
keyInsights: The squares in ∑ C(n,k)² are not intrinsic: they arise purely from the symmetry C(n,n-k) = C(n,k) applied to the second factor of Vandermonde's diagonal — the identity is really a self-convolution, not a sum of squares.

Working with the single symmetry lemma Nat.choose_symm_of_eq_add (n = a + b ⟹ C(n,a) = C(n,b)) keeps every step free of truncated ℕ-subtraction: each subtraction equality (n = ((n-d)-k)+(k+d) and 2n = (n-d)+(n+d)) is a one-line omega fact under d ≤ n.

Proving the shifted diagonal first and recovering the sum-of-squares as the d=0 corollary is strictly more general than proving the squares directly, at no extra cost — the same Vandermonde specialization handles both.
Stating the closed form as C(2n,n+d) rather than C(2n,n-d) (the two are equal by symmetry) makes the d=0 case land exactly on the central binomial coefficient C(2n,n).

The shifted diagonal has a clean double-counting reading: to select n+d objects from 2n split into two blocks of n, take k from the first block and n+d-k from the second; summing C(n,k)·C(n,n+d-k) = C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) over k recounts C(2n,n+d) — the algebraic Vandermonde specialization is the bijective count made formal.

sections.title: Proof Method Overview
sections.summary: The `## Method` block: specialize Vandermonde's Nat.add_choose_eq at m=n, r=n-d and route every rewrite through the single symmetry lemma Nat.choose_symm_of_eq_add, keeping the whole argument free of truncated ℕ-subtraction (each index split discharged by omega under d ≤ n). Sets up imports and the Nat/Finset API.

sections.title: Shifted Diagonal of Vandermonde
sections.summary: sum_choose_mul_choose_shift: for d ≤ n, ∑_{k=0}^{n-d} C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) = C(2n,n+d). Specializes Nat.add_choose_eq at m=n, r=n-d, converts the antidiagonal to a range sum, and folds C(n,(n-d)-k) to C(n,k+d) via Nat.choose_symm_of_eq_add, finishing with C(2n,n-d) = C(2n,n+d).

sections.title: Sum of Squares of a Binomial Row
sections.summary: sum_sq_choose: ∑_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k)² = C(2n,n), the d=0 diagonal — the sum of the squares of a Pascal row equals the central binomial coefficient. Obtained from the shifted diagonal at d=0 with simp [sq].

sections.title: Sanity Checks
sections.summary: Axiom-free decide verifications: ∑ C(3,k)² = 20 = C(6,3), ∑ C(4,k)² = 70 = C(8,4), and the shifted case ∑ C(4,k)·C(4,k+2) = 28 = C(8,6).

conclusion.summary: 2 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. The diagonal of Vandermonde's convolution is formalized in ℕ: the shifted self-convolution ∑_{k=0}^{n-d} C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) = C(2n,n+d) for d ≤ n, and its d=0 case, the classical sum-of-squares identity ∑_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k)² = C(2n,n).
conclusion.implications: This supplies the central-binomial identity ∑ C(n,k)² = C(2n,n) the gallery previously lacked (it held only the bound C(2n,n) ≤ 4^n and row log-concavity), completing the elementary Vandermonde suite alongside the general convolution (OQ-01) and the Chu–Vandermonde polynomial form (OQ-01-OQ-02). The single-symmetry, subtraction-free proof pattern transfers to any specialization C(m+n,r) where one row is rewritten by Pascal symmetry.
openQuestions: Does the weighted diagonal ∑_{k=0}^{n} k·C(n,k)² admit a comparably short closed form (n·C(2n-1,n-1)/... ) by combining this self-convolution with the first-moment absorption identity of OQ-09?

Can the shifted diagonal be lifted to a polynomial identity ∑_k C(n,k)·C(n,k+d) X^k over a commutative ring, recovering the integer statement at X=1, as the Chu–Vandermonde entry does for the general convolution?
